claim: The Triatominae are vectors for Trypanosoma cruzi, the aetiological agent of the neglected tropical Chagas disease.
source: The Triatominae are vectors for Trypanosoma cruzi, the aetiological agent of the neglected tropical Chagas disease.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the role of Triatominae in disease transmission.

claim: The distribution of Triatominae stretches across Latin America, with some species occurring outside of the Americas.
source: Their distribution stretches across Latin America, with some species occurring outside of the Americas.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the geographical distribution of Triatominae.

claim: Triatoma rubrofasciata has been detected in many Asian and African countries.
source: In particular, the cosmopolitan vector, Triatoma rubrofasciata, has already been detected in many Asian and African countries.
evidence: This is supported by observational data and references to detection records.

claim: An ensemble forecasting niche modelling approach was applied to project the climatic suitability of 11 triatomine species under current climate conditions on a global scale.
source: We applied an ensemble forecasting niche modelling approach to project the climatic suitability of 11 triatomine species under current climate conditions on a global scale.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Potential hotspots of triatomine species diversity are in tropical and subtropical regions between 21°N and 24°S latitude.
source: Our results revealed potential hotspots of triatomine species diversity in tropical and subtropical regions between 21°N and 24°S latitude.
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling results presented in the study.

claim: The climatic suitability of two temperate species (T. infestans, T. sordida) was determined in Europe, western Australia and New Zealand.
source: We also determined the climatic suitability of two temperate species (T. infestans, T. sordida) in Europe, western Australia and New Zealand.
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling results presented in the study.

claim: Triatoma rubrofasciata has been projected to find climatically suitable conditions in large parts of coastal areas throughout Latin America, Africa and Southeast Asia.
source: Triatoma rubrofasciata has been projected to find climatically suitable conditions in large parts of coastal areas throughout Latin America, Africa and Southeast Asia, emphasising the importance of an international vector surveillance program in these regions.
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling results presented in the study.

claim: The Triatominae comprise 152 species subdivided into 16 genera, including two fossils.
source: The Triatominae are haematophagous insects of the order Hemiptera and comprise 152 species subdivided into 16 genera, including two fossils (Poinar, 2013; Mendonça et al., 2016; da Rosa et al., 2017; Monteiro et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Triatomines are mainly distributed in Central and South America inhabiting environments ranging from tropical to temperate regions with cold winters.
source: Triatomines are mainly distributed in Central and South America inhabiting environments ranging from tropical to temperate regions with cold winters (de la Vega and Schilman, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Eleven species of Triatominae have been recorded in the southern United States.
source: Eleven species have also been recorded in the southern United States (Curtis-Robles et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Species belonging to the genus Linshcosteus occur in India.
source: In the Old World, species belonging to the genus Linshcosteus occur in India, whereas eight species of the genus Triatoma, especially the cosmopolitan T. rubrofasciata occur in Africa, the Middle-East, Southeast Asia, and in the Western Pacific (Gorla et al., 1997; Monteiro et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Eight species of the genus Triatoma occur in Africa, the Middle-East, Southeast Asia, and in the Western Pacific.
source: In the Old World, species belonging to the genus Linshcosteus occur in India, whereas eight species of the genus Triatoma, especially the cosmopolitan T. rubrofasciata occur in Africa, the Middle-East, Southeast Asia, and in the Western Pacific (Gorla et al., 1997; Monteiro et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Triatomines function as vectors for pathogens such as Trypanosoma conorhini, T. rangeli and T. cruzi.
source: Through their haematophagous lifestyle, triatomines function as vectors for pathogens such as Trypanosoma conorhini, T. rangeli and T. cruzi, the aetiological agent of Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis) (Deane and Deane, 1961; Ferreira et al., 2015; Vieira et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: T. cruzi is transmitted by infectious faeces of the triatomines, which are rubbed into the bite wound.
source: The flagellated protozoan parasite T. cruzi is transmitted by infectious faeces of the triatomines, which are rubbed into the bite wound.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the transmission mechanism of T. cruzi.

claim: Further transmission routes of T. cruzi include oral infection by the consumption of contaminated food or raw meat of infected mammalian hosts, congenital infection and transmission through blood transfusion or organ transplantation.
source: Further transmission routes include oral infection by the consumption of contaminated food or raw meat of infected mammalian hosts, congenital infection and transmission through blood transfusion or organ transplantation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about alternative transmission routes of T. cruzi.

claim: Acute symptoms of Chagas disease include fever, fatigue, headache, and myalgia.
source: Acute symptoms include fever, fatigue, headache, and myalgia, with long-term effects such as acute and chronic chagasic heart disease and gastrointestinal manifestations being more severe (Nóbrega et al., 2009; Coura and Viñas, 2010; Carlier et al., 2011; Rosas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Long-term effects of Chagas disease include acute and chronic chagasic heart disease and gastrointestinal manifestations.
source: Acute symptoms include fever, fatigue, headache, and myalgia, with long-term effects such as acute and chronic chagasic heart disease and gastrointestinal manifestations being more severe (Nóbrega et al., 2009; Coura and Viñas, 2010; Carlier et al., 2011; Rosas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Lee et al., 2013 calculated a global economic loss of $7.19 billion per year attributable to Chagas disease due to high health-care costs and lost productivity from early mortality.
source: Lee et al., 2013 calculated a global economic loss of $7.19 billion per year attributable to Chagas disease due to high health-care costs and lost productivity from early mortality.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: It is estimated that 6 to 7 million people worldwide are infected with Chagas disease, most of them living in Latin America.
source: It is estimated that 6 to 7 million people worldwide are infected with Chagas disease, most of them living in Latin America.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the prevalence of Chagas disease.

claim: Chagas disease has been increasingly detected in the United States, Canada, European and some Western Pacific countries due to global immigration and travel.
source: Caused by global immigration and travel, Chagas disease has been increasingly detected in the United States, Canada, European and some Western Pacific countries (WHO, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO data.

claim: There has been no vector-borne transmission of Chagas disease outside of the Americas due to the lack of vectors.
source: However, due to the lack of vectors, there has been no vector-borne transmission outside of the Americas.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the geographical limitation of vector-borne transmission.

claim: Triatomine bugs can be passively transported by the shipment of infested goods and animals or luggage and along air transportation routes.
source: Although the mobility of triatomine bugs is generally limited, they can be passively transported by the shipment of infested goods and animals or luggage and along air transportation routes (Fleming-Moran, 1992; Coura and Viñas, 2010; Pinto Dias, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Triatoma rubrofasciata is most widely distributed and recorded from the United States of America, Central and South America, coastal regions of Africa and the Middle-East, the Atlantic Ocean (Azores) and port areas of the Indo-Pacific region.
source: Among triatomine species, Triatoma rubrofasciata is most widely distributed and recorded from the United States of America, Central and South America, coastal regions of Africa and the Middle-East, the Atlantic Ocean (Azores) and port areas of the Indo-Pacific region (Dujardin et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: T. rubrofasciata is the only member of the Triatoma genus occurring in the New and Old World, with frequent records in previously non-endemic areas.
source: It is the only member of the Triatoma genus occurring in the New and Old World, with frequent records in previously non-endemic areas (Liu et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A New World origin of T. rubrofasciata seems more likely, although the evolutionary origin is unclear.
source: The evolutionary origin of T. rubrofasciata is unclear, although a New World origin seems more likely (Dujardin et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature and represents a speculative inference.

claim: T. rubrofasciata was spread along the shipping routes of the 16th to 19th century through its close association with domestic rats (especially Rattus rattus).
source: It is believed that through its close association with domestic rats (especially Rattus rattus), T. rubrofasciata was spread along the shipping routes of the 16th to 19th century (Schofield, 1988; Gorla et al., 1997; Patterson et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and represents a historical inference.

claim: T. rubrofasciata is able to transmit Trypanosoma cruzi in Latin America.
source: T. rubrofasciata is able to transmit Trypanosoma cruzi in Latin America; however, there are no records of vector transmission in the Old World (Dujardin et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: There are no records of T. rubrofasciata vector transmission in the Old World.
source: T. rubrofasciata is able to transmit Trypanosoma cruzi in Latin America; however, there are no records of vector transmission in the Old World (Dujardin et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Rhodnius prolixus was carried from Venezuela to Mexico and Central America by sea commerce and possibly by bird migration.
source: For instance, Rhodnius prolixus, one of the most important vectors of Chagas disease, was carried from Venezuela to Mexico and Central America by sea commerce and possibly by bird migration (Hashimoto and Schofield, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The potential spread of various triatomine species under current and future climatic conditions in South, Central and North America has been extensively studied.
source: The potential spread of various triatomine species under current and future climatic conditions in South, Central and North America has been extensively studied, but there is a lack of knowledge about climatic suitability outside the Americas (Gurgel-Gonçalves et al., 2012; Garza et al., 2014; Parra-Henao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There is a lack of knowledge about climatic suitability of triatomines outside the Americas.
source: The potential spread of various triatomine species under current and future climatic conditions in South, Central and North America has been extensively studied, but there is a lack of knowledge about climatic suitability outside the Americas (Gurgel-Gonçalves et al., 2012; Garza et al., 2014; Parra-Henao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and represents a knowledge gap.

claim: Ensemble forecasting approach is considered to yield robust estimations of the habitat suitability.
source: An ensemble forecasting approach was applied (Araújo and New, 2007), which is considered to yield robust estimations of the habitat suitability.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Rhodnius brethesi, R. ecuadoriensis and Triatoma maculata are limited to one or a few areas with mostly tropical climate.
source: Rhodnius brethesi, R. ecuadoriensis and Triatoma maculata are limited to one or a few areas with mostly tropical climate.
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling results presented in the study.

claim: Triatoma brasiliensis, Panstrongylus geniculatus, P. megistus, R. prolixus, T. dimidiata and T. rubrofasciata find suitable climate conditions in a broad range of tropical and sub-tropical regions.
source: Triatoma brasiliensis, Panstrongylus geniculatus, P. megistus, R. prolixus, T. dimidiata and T. rubrofasciata find suitable climate conditions in a broad range of tropical and sub-tropical regions, while T. sordida and T. infestans possess a broad potential range in temperate regions (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling results presented in the study and shown in Figure 1.

claim: T. sordida and T. infestans possess a broad potential range in temperate regions.
source: Triatoma brasiliensis, Panstrongylus geniculatus, P. megistus, R. prolixus, T. dimidiata and T. rubrofasciata find suitable climate conditions in a broad range of tropical and sub-tropical regions, while T. sordida and T. infestans possess a broad potential range in temperate regions (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling results presented in the study and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The projected range of R. brethesi is limited to areas with equatorial, tropical wet climate including the Amazon region in South America and Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Malaysia, New Guinea).
source: The projected range of R. brethesi and R. ecuadoriensis is limited to areas with equatorial, tropical wet climate. In the case of R. brethesi, these areas include, above all, the Amazon region in South America and Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Malaysia, New Guinea) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling results presented in the study and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: R. ecuadoriensis shows only a small modelled potential distribution in western Ecuador, parts of Indonesia, Malaysia and Papua-New Guinea as well as the Congo Basin.
source: R. ecuadoriensis shows only a small modelled potential distribution in western Ecuador, parts of Indonesia, Malaysia and Papua-New Guinea as well as the Congo Basin (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling results presented in the study and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: T. maculata possesses distribution potential under current climate conditions in the North of Brazil, Peru, Central Africa and parts of Southeast Asia (Malaysia, Indonesia, Philippines, New Guinea) beyond its observed distribution area in Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname and French Guiana.
source: Beyond its observed distribution area in Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname and French Guiana, T. maculata possesses distribution potential under current climate conditions in the North of Brazil, Peru, Central Africa and parts of Southeast Asia (Malaysia, Indonesia, Philippines, New Guinea) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling results presented in the study and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: T. brasiliensis has a modelled climatic distribution potential in southern West Africa, northern and southern Central Africa and East Africa beyond eastern Brazil.
source: T. brasiliensis prefers dry and wet savannah climate as found in eastern Brazil. Furthermore, this species has a modelled climatic distribution potential in southern West Africa, northern and southern Central Africa and East Africa (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling results presented in the study and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Models project large climatically suitable areas for P. geniculatus, P. megistus, R. prolixus and T. dimidiata in tropical regions in South America, Central America, Caribbean, Central and East Africa, eastern Madagascar, in the South of India and Sri Lanka and throughout Southeast Asia.
source: Models project large climatically suitable areas for P. geniculatus, P. megistus, R. prolixus and T. dimidiata in tropical regions in South America, Central America, Caribbean, Central and East Africa, eastern Madagascar, in the South of India and Sri Lanka and throughout Southeast Asia (Figure 1E–H).
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling results presented in the study and shown in Figure 1E-H.

claim: The climatic suitability models of T. infestans show extensive potential spread in semi-arid to humid and temperate to cold regions comprising the Southern Cone of South America, parts of Brazil, Bolivia and Peru, Mexico, Caribbean and Florida (USA), the South of Africa, parts of the Arabian Peninsula, the West and South of Australia, New Zealand and in Europe Portugal, Spain, France, Italy, Greece, Ireland and Great Britain.
source: The climatic suitability models of the latter show extensive potential spread in both semi-arid to humid and temperate to cold regions comprising the Southern Cone of South America, parts of Brazil, Bolivia and Peru, Mexico, Caribbean and Florida (USA), the South of Africa, parts of the Arabian Peninsula, the West and South of Australia, New Zealand and in Europe Portugal, Spain, France, Italy, Greece, Ireland and Great Britain (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling results presented in the study and shown in Figure 1J.

claim: For T. rubrofasciata, primarily coastal regions in tropical savannah and monsoon areas were predicted as climatically suitable including the east coast of South America and Central America, large parts of Brazil and Venezuela, Caribbean, Florida (USA), the coasts of Central and Eastern Africa, the eastern coast of Madagascar, southern India and Sri Lanka, Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia, Vietnam, southern China and Japan, Philippines and the eastern coast of Australia.
source: For T. rubrofasciata, primarily coastal regions in tropical savannah and monsoon areas were predicted as climatically suitable including the east coast of South America and Central America, large parts of Brazil and Venezuela, Caribbean, Florida (USA), the coasts of Central and Eastern Africa, the eastern coast of Madagascar, southern India and Sri Lanka, Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia, Vietnam, southern China and Japan, Philippines and the eastern coast of Australia (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling results presented in the study and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The observed occurrence of the considered species is mainly consistent with the projected climatic suitability in Latin America.
source: The observed occurrence of the considered species is mainly consistent with the projected climatic suitability in Latin America.
evidence: This is an evaluation of the model results against observed data.

claim: For some species the modelled climate suitability in Central and South America exceeds the area of current occurrence.
source: Nevertheless, it is noteworthy that for some species the modelled climate suitability in Central and South America exceeds the area of current occurrence.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing model results with observed data.

claim: T. dimidiata is not observed in large parts of Brazil, Peru and Bolivia, although a good climatic suitability has been projected.
source: For example, T. dimidiata is not observed in large parts of Brazil, Peru and Bolivia, although a good climatic suitability has been projected (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing model results with observed data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The quantity of triatomine species varies between zero and seven in different regions.
source: The quantity of species varies between zero and seven.
evidence: This is a finding from the species diversity analysis.

claim: Areas of great triatomine diversity have foremost tropical forest and savannah-like climate and include predominantly regions between 21°N and 24°S latitude.
source: Areas of great triatomine diversity have foremost tropical forest and savannah-like climate and include predominantly regions between 21°N and 24°S latitude (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the species diversity analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Even in temperate regions, some species could find suitable climatic conditions, for example in Portugal, Spain and eastern Australia.
source: However, even in temperate regions, some species could find suitable climatic conditions, for example in Portugal, Spain and eastern Australia.
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling results.

claim: The most important bioclimatic variable is the temperature seasonality (BIO4) for all considered species.
source: The most important bioclimatic variable is the temperature seasonality (BIO4) for all considered species, closely followed by the minimum temperature of the coldest month (BIO6) and maximum temperature of the warmest month (BIO5).
evidence: This is a finding from the variable importance analysis.

claim: The minimum temperature of the coldest month (BIO6) and maximum temperature of the warmest month (BIO5) closely follow temperature seasonality in importance.
source: The most important bioclimatic variable is the temperature seasonality (BIO4) for all considered species, closely followed by the minimum temperature of the coldest month (BIO6) and maximum temperature of the warmest month (BIO5).
evidence: This is a finding from the variable importance analysis.

claim: The three precipitation variables (BIO13, BIO14, and BIO15) seem to shape the species distribution in a subordinate way.
source: The three precipitation variables (BIO13, BIO14, and BIO15) seem to shape the species distribution in a subordinate way.
evidence: This is a finding from the variable importance analysis.

claim: Almost all actual occurrence points of T. rubrofasciata (with coordinates provided) are within an area classified as climatically suitable by the models.
source: The evaluation of the global projection of the climatic suitability shows that almost all actual occurrence points of T. rubrofasciata (with coordinates provided) are within an area classified as climatically suitable by the models (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the model validation analysis.

claim: A few occurrence points of T. rubrofasciata are located in areas projected as less suitable including seaports such as Singapore and the Okinawa islands in Japan.
source: A few occurrence points are located in areas projected as less suitable including seaports such as Singapore and the Okinawa islands in Japan.
evidence: This is a finding from the model validation analysis.

claim: Every country in which T. rubrofasciata has been found (but without specific coordinates of occurrence records given) provides at least one area offering suitable climatic conditions.
source: According to the models, every country in which T. rubrofasciata has been found (but without specific coordinates of occurrence records given) provides at least one area offering suitable climatic conditions, for example Indonesia, Madagascar and several African countries.
evidence: This is a finding from the model validation analysis.

claim: The discriminatory capacity of all models displays a good predictive performance, which is also reflected in the AUC values of over 0.9.
source: The discriminatory capacity of all models displays a good predictive performance, which is also reflected in the AUC values of over 0.9.
evidence: This is a finding from the model evaluation.

claim: GBM (generalised boosted models) performs particularly well for all species and achieves the highest AUC values.
source: GBM (generalised boosted models) performs particularly well for all species and achieves the highest AUC values – the same applies to GAM (generalized additive models).
evidence: This is a finding from the model evaluation.

claim: GAM (generalized additive models) performs particularly well for all species and achieves the highest AUC values.

claim: Slightly lower AUC values are generated by ANN (artificial neuronal networks) and MAXENT (maximum entropy).
source: Slightly lower AUC values are generated by ANN (artificial neuronal networks) and MAXENT (maximum entropy) (Supplementary file 2, Supplementary file 3).

claim: R. brethesi is closely associated with palm trees and features prominently in the sylvatic transmission of Trypanosoma cruzi feeding particularly on opossums (Didelphis spp.).
source: For instance, R. brethesi is closely associated with palm trees and features prominently in the sylvatic transmission of Trypanosoma cruzi feeding particularly on opossums (Didelphis spp.). Domestic or peri-domestic behaviour is not observed, thus, R. brethesis' domestic vector potential is most likely low (Coura et al., 2002; Rocha et al., 2004).

claim: Domestic or peri-domestic behaviour is not observed in R. brethesi, thus, R. brethesis' domestic vector potential is most likely low.

Domestic or peri-domestic behaviour is not observed, thus, R. brethesis' domestic vector potential is most likely low (Coura et al., 2002; Rocha et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and represents an inference.

claim: Rhodnius ecuadoriensis is distributed in southern Ecuador and northern Peru, where it exhibits domestic and peri-domestic behaviour invading chicken coops and human dwellings.
source: Rhodnius ecuadoriensis is distributed in southern Ecuador and northern Peru, where it exhibits domestic and peri-domestic behaviour invading chicken coops and human dwellings. In the sylvatic environment, R. ecuadoriensis is mainly found in palm trees (Phytelephas aequatorialis) (Abad-Franch et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: R. ecuadoriensis establishes dense populations and is commonly infected with T. cruzi indicating a high vector potential.
source: Rhodnius ecuadoriensis is distributed in southern Ecuador and northern Peru, where it exhibits domestic and peri-domestic behaviour invading chicken coops and human dwellings. It establishes dense populations and is commonly infected with T. cruzi indicating a high vector potential. In the sylvatic environment, R. ecuadoriensis is mainly found in palm trees (Phytelephas aequatorialis) (Abad-Franch et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature and represents an inference about vector potential.

claim: In the sylvatic environment, R. ecuadoriensis is mainly found in palm trees (Phytelephas aequatorialis).

It establishes dense populations and is commonly infected with T. cruzi indicating a high vector potential. claim: The T. cruzi infection rate of Triatoma maculata depends on the geographical area.
source: The T. cruzi infection rate of Triatoma maculata depends on the geographical area. In most regions T. maculata has ornithophilic feeding preferences, whereas studies in the Colombian Caribbean region reported active transmission in peri-domestic human dwellings involving dogs as reservoir hosts (Cantillo-Barraza et al., 2014; Cantillo-Barraza et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In most regions T. maculata has ornithophilic feeding preferences.
source: The T. cruzi infection rate of Triatoma maculata depends on the geographical area. In most regions T. maculata has ornithophilic feeding preferences, whereas studies in the Colombian Caribbean region reported active transmission in peri-domestic human dwellings involving dogs as reservoir hosts (Cantillo-Barraza et al., 2014; Cantillo-Barraza et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Studies in the Colombian Caribbean region reported active transmission of T. cruzi by T. maculata in peri-domestic human dwellings involving dogs as reservoir hosts.
source: The T. cruzi infection rate of Triatoma maculata depends on the geographical area. evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Triatoma brasiliensis is located in tropical savannah regions with a hot and dry climate altering with intensive rain.
source: Triatoma brasiliensis is located in tropical savannah regions with a hot and dry climate altering with intensive rain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the habitat of T. brasiliensis.

claim: T. brasiliensis is found under rock piles feeding on a broad range of reptile and mammalian hosts, including humans.

claim: Triatoma brasiliensis is considered as an important vector for Chagas disease due to its high Trypanosoma cruzi infection and intradomiciliary infestation rates.
source: Due to its high Trypanosoma cruzi infection and intradomiciliary infestation rates, Triatoma brasiliensis is considered as an important vector for Chagas disease (Carcavallo et al., 1997).

claim: Panstrongylus geniculatus is described as eurythermic and adapted to several dry as well as humid ecotopes.
source: The climatic niche of Panstrongylus geniculatus was projected to be very broad (Figure 1E). A result that is reinforced by the literature in which the species is described as eurythermic and adapted to several dry as well as humid ecotopes (Patterson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

source: It feeds on the blood of various hosts, such as marsupials, opossums, anteaters, armadillos, bats, cats, birds and chicken, in whose nests and coops it can be found. Additionally, it invades human houses and possesses a high susceptibility to Trypanosoma cruzi (Feliciangeli et al., 2004).

claim: P. geniculatus invades human houses and possesses a high susceptibility to Trypanosoma cruzi.
source: It feeds on the blood of various hosts, such as marsupials, opossums, anteaters, armadillos, bats, cats, birds and chicken, in whose nests and coops it can be found. Additionally, it invades human houses and possesses a high susceptibility to Trypanosoma cruzi (Feliciangeli et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: R. prolixus is an anthropophilic species which permanently colonises human dwellings.
source: Similar climatic distribution patterns are shown by the anthropophilic species R. prolixus, which permanently colonises human dwellings (Rabinovich et al., 2011).

claim: P. megistus occurs primarily in the Atlantic rain forests of South America and requires high relative humidity for breeding.
source: P. megistus occurs primarily in the Atlantic rain forests of South America and requires high relative humidity for breeding.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the habitat requirements of P. megistus.

claim: The modelled distribution of P. megistus is highly influenced by the bioclimatic variable describing the maximum temperature of the warmest month (BIO5).
source: With exception of the triatomine species occurring in temperate climate regions, solely the modelled distribution of P. megistus is highly influenced by the bioclimatic variable describing the maximum temperature of the warmest month (BIO5). claim: P. megistus is strongly limited by arid climates.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature and represents a speculative explanation.

claim: T. infestans is adapted to deal with cold temperatures and has a greater diversity of wild habitats, which is probably related to the behavioural plasticity of the species.
